extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, math researchers, graduate students, and readers interested in mathematical practice and exposition (including in the AI era)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging the quality and value of mathematical proofs and expository writing, emphasizing human-centered virtues (clarity, conceptual invention, truth-seeking, and exposure of process) rather than mere mechanical correctness. Framed as guidance for practicing mathematicians and readers assessing mathematical work, especially in an era of AI-generated output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity and insight. Expert proofs make "main ideas, obstructions to be overcome, etc." identifiable; weak proofs (e.g. AI-generated ones) often obscure the reasoning path entirely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good proof should make its main ideas and the key obstructions explicit so a reader can see why the argument works. Anti-patterns include proofs that are mechanically correct but hide the reasoning path, or that read like a sequence of manipulations without showing which steps were conceptual pivots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful conceptualisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Humans "develop useful new objects, terminology, etc. to capture what they're doing" — creating lasting conceptual frameworks beyond mere argument execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuate the creation of useful concepts, definitions, and language that clarify and generalize phenomena. Prefer work that introduces notions that persist as tools for further thought rather than ad hoc maneuvers that only serve a single calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth-seeking orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics depends on practitioners being "by and large truth-seeking" — not generating persuasive-sounding but false claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the author genuinely seeks correct understanding rather than polished persuasion. Be wary of outputs that prioritize sounding convincing (or producing the desired conclusion) over honest verification; this matters especially when AI can synthesize plausible but incorrect arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asking the right questions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Mathematics isn't only about saying true things. It's about asking the right questions, being confused, stumbling about, getting distracted, being wrong, recognizing when you're wrong, being stuck."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge contributions by the importance and appropriateness of the questions posed: does the work identify questions that advance understanding or open productive directions? Value taste and judgment in selecting problems as part of mathematical quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embodied struggle and intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Math involves embodied struggle — developing intuition by repeated engagement until comprehension emerges through accumulated contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and reward evidence that the author has engaged deeply and developed intuition (examples, heuristics, motivations) rather than presenting only polished final statements. The process of struggle and iterative engagement is a legitimate part of mathematical value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research value / theory-building
rubrics_metrics.description: Proving existing lemmas is only a portion of math. The harder work is "discovering the statements of crucial lemmas" — theory-building, taste, asking which questions matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work contributes to theory (new statements, organizing principles, or frameworks) rather than merely executing routine proofs. Prioritize originality in identifying and formulating the meaningful intermediate results that enable further progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose the author's process (confusion, scaffolding, obstructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A "good" piece of mathematical writing exposes (a) what the author was confused about, (b) which conceptual scaffolding they built, (c) which obstructions they overcame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good exposition makes the writer's process visible: what was puzzling, what constructions or viewpoints were introduced to overcome obstacles, and which difficulties remained. This transparency helps readers internalize methods and judgments; concealment of process reduces pedagogical and epistemic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical correctness is necessary but not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Polished mechanical correctness is necessary but not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While formal correctness is a baseline requirement, do not equate correctness with mathematical goodness. A piece that is technically correct but lacks insight, conceptualization, question-sensitivity, or process transparency should be judged as incomplete or lower-quality.
